title: Felix Manz (1527)
hook: baptized as adults, an early Anabaptist martyr is drowned by other Protestants

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zwingli's sausages, and a question about rules that spread through Zurich. Your line was why do we do this? What did you find when you asked it? Day eight hundred sixty.

A small boat pushes out into the river that runs through Zurich. In it is a young man with his hands bound. His name is Felix Manz. He had studied with Zwingli, read the Bible with him, cheered the questions Zwingli raised. And he took those questions one step further than the city would allow. Now the city council of Zurich, a Protestant council in a Protestant city, has sentenced him to be drowned. The accounts say he sang as they took him out. Today's word is the name opponents gave to him and his friends: Anabaptist.
screen: `A BOAT ON THE RIVER IN ZURICH.`

segments.voice: Here's the step. Manz and a circle of friends, Conrad Grebel among them, read the New Testament and noticed that the baptisms there follow faith. People hear, believe, and then are baptized. So they asked: shouldn't baptism come after a person can confess faith for themselves? And they began baptizing one another as adults, in a house in Zurich. Their opponents called them Anabaptists, re-baptizers, because they had already been baptized as infants. They didn't accept the name. To them, this was their first real baptism. The council outlawed it. Manz was arrested, released, arrested again, and finally drowned in the river. Christians to this day answer the baptism question differently, and both answers have deep roots. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist churches baptize infants, seeing baptism as God's gift and promise, given before a child can ask. Mennonites, Baptists and others baptize those who confess faith themselves. But Manz's circle held something else too. They refused to take up the sword, even to defend themselves, and early Anabaptist confessions said so plainly. Their picture came from the prophet Isaiah, who sees a world where, in the King James words, "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb." And: "They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain." The peaceable kingdom. It's a hard thing to sit with. In those years, Christians put other Christians to death over how and when to baptize. Manz was killed by a city whose reformers had once read the Bible beside him. And he went to the river still believing that followers of Jesus should never hurt anyone.
screen: `THE WOLF SHALL DWELL WITH THE LAMB.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember those persecuted by other Christians. Start with Felix Manz in the boat. Then widen it. Anabaptists. Catholics. Protestants. Orthodox Christians. In more than one place and time, Christians have suffered at the hands of other Christians, and some still do. Hold them in mind, without needing to decide who was most to blame. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for those who hurt them. If you don't, just keep them company in silence for a while. The bell holds the time.
Anabaptist. A name opponents gave to Christians who baptized adults on their own confession of faith. Felix Manz's circle also refused the sword.
Your line: the peaceable kingdom. Today, in one argument you'd normally win by force of words, choose not to hurt. Day eight hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Mennonite, Amish, Hutterite and other Anabaptist-descended churches baptize those who confess faith for themselves and remember their early martyrs, including Felix Manz, and nonviolence is part of their heritage.

options: keep quiet and go back to the city church.
fork.reveal: he kept going, was arrested again, and was drowned in the river. the accounts say he sang on the way.

what a scholar hears: the radical reformation in Zurich, and early Anabaptist confessions that placed the sword outside the life of Christ's followers.
